articles.title: Midterms are bad for incumbents – and even worse when energy prices are high
articles.author: Michael A. Mische, Associate Professor of the Practice of Management and Organization, Marshall School of Business, University of Southern California
paras: As Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “It’s the economy, stupid.” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. The cost of energy underlies much of the economy, making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise.
Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D.C.

Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think, because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers, with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on.
When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food, follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally.

Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection. For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record.
Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections.
Oil embargo, Nixon and Ford

Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States. OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month, and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4.31 to $10.31 per barrel in March 1974. Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U.S. gasoline prices from increasing 32%.
When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. Inflation was 12.3%, and gas prices were still high.
Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “Whip Inflation Now,” or WIN, campaign. But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats.
“WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter.
In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. stayed high and even climbed slightly. Inflation hit 9% in 1978.

In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats. Inflation continued to climb, and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976. Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan.

Reagan implemented “Reaganomics” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum. By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U.S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut, lowering the average price of crude oil and U.S. gasoline price from previous highs.
In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate.

Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate.

In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And gas prices were up 22%. In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate.

Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy. U.S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40%. Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups.
And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon.
Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies.

Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0.17 to $0.42 per gallon.

But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project that would have brought more petroleum into the U.S. and suspended new oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also recommitted the U.S. to the Paris climate accord, under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source.
In June 2022, inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high. And U.S. gasoline prices reached an all-time high of $4.929 per gallon; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5.60 a gallon today.

The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party lost nine House seats and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that energy prices aren’t the only factor in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots.

During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, crude oil prices fell 4.5%, U.S. oil production rose 3.3%, from 13.3 million to 13.7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4.5%, from $3.12 to $2.98 per gallon.

On Feb. 28, 2026, U.S. military action against Iran disrupted Middle Eastern oil production and oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Initially, shipment volume plummeted, though by the end of September it had recovered to 82% to 92% of prewar levels.

Overall, Middle Eastern crude oil exports are averaging around 24 million barrels a day, exceeding prewar levels in part because of increased use of pipelines out of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Because of the war with Iran, AAA’s national average price of unleaded regular gasoline has increased by almost 40%, from February’s $2.98 price to $4.15 a gallon as of Nov. 3, 2026.
As the preelection polling had suggested, voters held Trump accountable for high gasoline and grocery prices, as well as an unpopular war.

It was a reminder of a basic economic and political principle: When the economy is doing well, voters are more likely to support incumbents and their parties. And when voters are pessimistic about the economy’s future, they are inclined to vote against incumbents and their parties.

articles.title: ‘Epic’ blue wave helps Democrats take Congress in overwhelming rebuke to President Trump
articles.author: Charlie Hunt, Associate Professor of Political Science, Boise State University
paras: Voters turned out in massive numbers on Election Day to hand Democrats control of Congress, in a sweeping snub of President Donald Trump and Republicans. Democrats won several statewide races in places long considered GOP bastions, including races that were considered insurmountable even weeks ago.

Democrats took control of the House and Senate, flipping Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Kansas and Ohio. The results reflected broad dissatisfaction across the country with Trump, his agenda and the candidates he had endorsed.
The Conversation’s senior politics editor, Alfonso Serrano, spoke on election night with Charlie Hunt, a scholar at Boise State University who studies Congress and elections.

It was obviously a strong showing for Democrats on Election Day, something that was even evident in the margin of some Democratic losses. What does it tell you, for example, that democratic socialist Angie Nixon fought a competitive race for the Senate in Florida?

There is this big uniform shift toward the Democrats that we’re seeing really across virtually all kinds of locations and geographies and counties. What I think is particularly notable here, and something we were on the lookout for in this election, and we’re seeing it, is the substantial shift in the Hispanic vote from 2024 in places like Texas and Florida, where you’re getting these 30-to-35 point shifts from how Donald Trump performed in 2024. That was a big part of what helped him win, and it seems like it has snapped right back and even farther in the other direction. This is what made Florida, I think, closer than a lot of folks thought.

It’s what put a number of really, really right-leaning districts in play, particularly in South Florida. And it looks like it is going to help Democrats keep the number of seats they had in Florida in the House that they had before the election, which is incredible when you consider that Florida did this mid-decade gerrymander to try to get them out of a bunch of those seats.

Some rural areas of the country were also more competitive than expected, like North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, where Democrat Jaime Ager flipped a conservative district. What does that tell you?

It’s definitely an indicator of at least one of these two things. One is just really massive Democratic turnout across the board. Regardless of where they live, Democrats were so enthusiastic and energized to turn out that they did so across all different types of districts and counties.

It could also be an indicator of some cross-party voting, where Republicans are crossing over in some cases and voting for the Democrat. I don’t imagine there’s a ton of that, but in a lot of these close districts, and if you’ve got enough of those folks in places like Texas, it really does make a big difference, those small shifts.

I think we’re probably also likely to see, and we saw some of this in the exit polling, a major shift in independent voters, unaffiliated voters, toward the Democrats, whereas in 2024 they had been closer to Trump.

I’d like to go back to turnout briefly. Turnout looks like it was strong across the country. In Georgia, for example, Election Day’s turnout was on pace to beat turnout in the 2024 presidential elections.

That’s unprecedented, at least in modern elections. In Texas, for example, in some counties we saw James Talarico getting as many raw votes as Kamala Harris did in a presidential election. This isn’t a very political science term, but that’s insane. In a midterm election you typically see 10% or 15% less turnout than you would in a presidential election. But Democrats voted in presidential-level numbers in a lot of these really key areas, and that’s explaining how they’re able to overperform at levels we haven’t seen in at least 20 years.

Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars supporting Republican candidates, including some US$200 million in Texas to elect Ken Paxton for the Senate, who lost. What does that tell you about the influence of political spending?

Republican PACs, super PACs and billionaire donors like Elon Musk may have raised more money compared to Democrats, but Democratic candidates themselves outraised Republican candidates through donors that gave directly to their campaigns.

This is important for a couple of reasons. Number one, because candidates get much better rates on TV ad buys than outside spenders. And so they get more bang for their buck when they’re spending on advertisements, which is the most expensive component of any campaign. And more to the point, that is an indicator of sort of dedicated grassroots donors who turn into voters, whereas Musk gets one vote at the end of the day.

And there is no amount of money that can make up for a really flawed candidate like Ken Paxton. And more to the point, a lot of this money, once you get into the tens, the hundreds of millions of dollars, a lot of the research talks about the diminishing returns that you get on that. Going from zero dollars spent to $10 million spent, that’s a very different kind of campaign. But once you go from $500 million to $510 million, that’s not going to get you a whole lot more votes.

The territory that Democrats covered is unbelievable. The South Carolina Senate race went to Annie Andrews, the Democrat, which was unfathomable even a few months ago. Mississippi still appears to be somewhat in play. The blue wave turned into something approaching a tsunami. I think a lot of Democrats saw the polling and didn’t want to believe it or couldn’t bring themselves to believe it. But some of this late polling seems to have gotten things on the mark.

What we’ve seen in these midterm elections is a massive rebuke of the last two years of the Trump administration, and a sort of blue wave of epic proportions toward the Democrats, the likes of which we haven’t seen in 20 or more years. It’s a huge confirmation of the approach that Democrats took in this election.

articles.title: Democrats in House poised to investigate the Trump Administration, taking up a long-standing power GOP-led Congress ignored for the past two years
articles.author: Drew Kurlowski, Associate Professor of Political Science, Coastal Carolina University
paras: Oversight is coming for the Trump administration.

That’s been the message of congressional Democrats throughout the closing days of the 2026 midterm campaign. Now that the party’s candidates have reportedly won control of the House of Representatives, that campaign promise is likely to be carried out. Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin told The New York Times in late October that among the potential oversight targets were pardons granted by President Donald Trump, possible corruption in government contracting and the Trump family’s cryptocurrency deals.
Routine congressional oversight hearings usually don’t make headlines.
That changed during the second Trump administration.
When Attorney General Pam Bondi appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Oct. 7, 2025, what took place was a contentious, highly partisan, made-for-TV-and-social-media confrontation.
Bondi refused to answer many questions from Democrats, instead launching personal attacks against these members of the U.S. Senate.
The episode captures a basic tension in congressional oversight: Congress can demand answers, but getting them often depends on the cooperation of the branch it is investigating.
That tension is about to sharpen when Democrats control the oversight process. Their hearings will likely be anything but routine.
From our perspective as political scientists who study the U.S. Congress, congressional oversight has played an important role in American democracy. Here’s a brief history.

In simple terms, oversight is the ability of Congress to ensure that the laws it passes are faithfully executed. This generally means asking questions, demanding information, convening hearings and holding the executive branch accountable for its actions.

Oversight isn’t specifically mentioned in the Constitution. Article 1, Section 8, which lists the powers of Congress, includes the power “to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper,” without identifying an oversight role. Once laws are enacted, Article 2, Section 3, states that the president “shall take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed.”

However, the framers viewed congressional oversight as a key component of legislative authority. They wanted presidents to take Congress seriously and structured the Constitution to ensure that the executive would be accountable to the legislature.

As James Madison urged in Federalist 51, the separate branches of government should have the power to keep each other from becoming too powerful. “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition,” Madison wrote.

The framers drew from the examples of the British Parliament and Colonial legislatures. In 1621, Sir Francis Bacon was charged with corruption and impeached as Lord High Chancellor after an investigation by a committee of the British Parliament. And in 1768, the Massachusetts Assembly conducted an investigation of Gov. Francis Bernard that led to a formal request to the King of England for his removal.

At the Federal Convention in 1787 that produced the Constitution, Delegate George Mason noted that members of Congress possessed “inquisitory powers” and “must meet frequently to inspect the Conduct of public officials.” Even though this idea was never written down, it was a habit of self-government that early Congresses put into practice.

Congressional oversight began almost as soon as the first Congress met. In 1790, Robert Morris, the superintendent of finances during the Continental Congress and a financier of the American Revolution, asked Congress to investigate his handling of the country’s finances and was exonerated of any wrongdoing.

During this period, congressional investigations were often referred to select committees – bodies created to perform special functions. These panels had the power to issue subpoenas and hold individuals in contempt. Since there was no official record of debates and proceedings, the public relied on newspaper accounts to learn about what had happened.

In March 1792, congressional oversight exposed businessman William Duer, who signed contracts with the War Department but failed to furnish the needed military supplies. This shortfall contributed to a stunning U.S. military defeat against a confederation of Native American tribes in the Northwest Territory.
Congress eventually removed the quartermaster general from his role for mismanaging the contracts.
Throughout the 19th century, Congress continued to quietly exercise this power.

Hearings from December 1861 to May 1865 on the conduct of the U.S. Civil War produced a detailed record of the war, exposed military wrongdoing and condemned slavery. In 1871, the Senate created a select committee to investigate Ku Klux Klan violence during Reconstruction.
Investigating corruption and criminal acts
Congress started to use its oversight power more aggressively in the 1920s with the Senate Committee on Public Land and Surveys’ high-profile investigations into the Teapot Dome scandal.

Hearings revealed that Interior Secretary Albert Bacon Fall had secretly leased federal oil reserves in Wyoming to two private corporations and had received personal loans and gifts from the companies in return.
The investigation found clear evidence of corruption. Fall was indicted and became the first U.S. Cabinet member to be convicted of a felony.

The U.S. Supreme Court helped to shape the legal foundation of congressional oversight. In McGrain v. Daugherty, decided in 1927, the court held that congressional committees could issue subpoenas, force witnesses to testify and hold them in contempt if they fail to appear. Two years later, in Sinclair v. United States, the court ruled that witnesses who lied to Congress could be charged with perjury.
These cases granted the judicial branch’s sanction to what had long been an implied legislative power, cementing the constitutionality of congressional oversight.
The modern era of congressional oversight has produced some very important reforms – and some truly regrettable spectacles.

The most important example of bipartisan congressional oversight came in response to reporting by The Washington Post’s Carl Bernstein and Bob Woodward. The two journalists wrote about the 1972 burgling of Democratic National Committee offices in Washington, D.C.’s Watergate Hotel and subsequent cover-up efforts by the Nixon administration – and President Richard Nixon himself.

On Feb. 7, 1973, the U.S. Senate voted 77-0 to establish a Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, which brought together Democrats and Republicans to investigate what came to be known as the “Watergate scandal.” The committee’s work spurred action in Congress to impeach Nixon, leading to Nixon’s resignation in 1974 and to the enactment of legal reforms to provide an institutional check on presidential power.

Another high point for congressional oversight came after the 9/11 terrorist attacks in 2001. Seeking to learn how the deadliest terrorist strike on American soil had occurred, Democratic Sen. Bob Graham and Republican Rep. Porter Goss, who chaired the Senate and House Intelligence committees, formed a joint committee to investigate intelligence failures before and after the attacks.

This inquiry produced several important recommendations that were ultimately adopted, including the creation of a director of national intelligence and a Department of Homeland Security, as well as better information sharing among law enforcement agencies.

Congress’ oversight can extend beyond the executive branch when the actions of private actors raise questions about existing laws or spur the need for new ones. Investigations into medical device safety and Enron’s 2001 collapse examined malfeasance in the private sphere that existing regulations failed to prevent.

However, the power to expose corruption can also be used as a tool to score partisan points and generate outrage, rather than holding the executive branch accountable for actual malfeasance. Notably, in the 1950s, Wisconsin Sen. Joseph McCarthy turned oversight into inquisition and used the power of media to amplify his accusations of communist influence within the federal government.

As we see it, the problem with allowing oversight to become political theater is that it distracts Congress from quieter and more meaningful oversight work. Slow, procedural work isn’t likely to go viral, but it helps keep government accountable. The task of a deliberate legislative body is to reconcile those very different impulses.
Congressional oversight has strengthened the democratic system at many points. But it can also be stymied by an uncooperative executive branch.

After the 2018 midterm elections put Democrats in charge of the House of Representatives, their many attempts to exercise oversight were rejected by the first Trump administration, which refused to send officials to testify at hearings, failed to turn over documents and ignored subpoenas.
Will the next two years of divided government look the same?
This is an updated version of a story originally published on Nov. 6, 2025.

articles.title: Justice Department’s interference before midterms was unsuccessful, unprofessional and unprecedented
articles.author: John E. Jones III, President, Dickinson College
paras: From Washington, D.C. to Anchorage, Alaska, federal courts have been busy with cases related to the Trump administration’s attempts to assert control over state elections. In almost every case, rulings have gone against the administration. But despite the fears of many Democrats, there was no mayhem launched by the Trump administration on Election Day.

One federal judge chastised administration officials for being “engaged in a campaign to intimidate, threaten and coerce state and local officials and employees who are engaged in administering the ongoing midterm 2026 election.” Another wrote with umbrage that “If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger.” And the nation’s highest court, the Supreme Court, in what The New York Times called “an extraordinary rebuke,” refused to intervene in the administration’s appeal of a lower court ruling that barred federal intervention in California ballot counting.

The Conversation’s politics and legal affairs editor, Naomi Schalit, spoke on Election Day with Dickinson College President John Jones, a former federal judge, about the Trump administration’s actions – and how judges see them.
What are you seeing with all these cases?

The common stripe in every one of the cases that have been decided close to the election is that courts are reluctant to get involved after voting has started. And I think the courts’ perspectives are clearly affected by the high number of early votes cast either in person before Election Day or using mail-in voting. Without question, we’ve already been in the midst of this election – from a voting standpoint – for some time, and courts simply don’t want to get in the way of that and disrupt the process.
The court opinions haven’t been only about how they don’t want to get involved. They’re also saying to the Justice Department, “You shouldn’t be taking a role here as well.”

That’s right. And of course it harkens back to what I’ve said before, which is that Article 1, Section 4 of the Constitution gives the states the power to regulate elections. Congress has some license to legislate in matters relating to national elections, but notably absent from Section 4 is any role for the executive branch to play.

All of the cases have that perspective. But as you go case by case, even assuming that the administration could, for example, sell its allegation that there are 20,000 suspect ballots in California and that the administration has an interest in those ballots, it’s simply too close to the election. There is something called the Purcell Principle, based on a Supreme Court precedent, that federal courts as a rule should not wade into election controversies at a point in time that’s too close to when they’re being conducted.
What does the string of administration losses in these cases tell you about the leadership at the Department of Justice?

I believe that the Department of Justice has become completely unmoored from its mission. Recall that in 2016, very close to the presidential election, then-FBI Director James Comey revealed the investigation into candidate Hillary Clinton’s emails.

It was seen as a tremendous breach of protocol by the Department of Justice. And look at where we are today, where it has now become the norm for the Department of Justice to take action so close to the election.

Just today, for example, we know that target letters were sent out by the Department of Justice to numerous individuals allegedly involved in the Alaska controversy that placed a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot. There were a thousand or so election watchers dispatched to polling places by the Department of Justice – these are unprecedented numbers.

Then there were the lawsuits that were filed by the Department of Justice close to the election. This was forbidden territory for the DOJ before this election cycle, and it’s now become business as usual.
It was forbidden territory because the idea was that – unlike most of the other executive agencies – the DOJ had a kind of holy, nonpolitical status?

The central idea, I think, is that the Department of Justice would not want to put its thumb on the scale and affect an election, particularly if there’s an investigation that is announced and isn’t closed.

To reveal an investigation – or investigations, as they’ve done in several cases now – means that some will take that as meaning there has been criminal misconduct when that obviously may not be the case at all. This is a further weaponization of the Department of Justice, in my view, that I find unconscionable.

And given how clumsy its efforts have been, this is clearly the leadership of the Department of Justice acceding to the wishes of the president of the United States even when there is no sound legal basis to proceed. A lot of this has been very unprofessionally done and strains both the reputation and credibility of the Department of Justice and the lawyers that it’s sending in front of federal judges.

Given the number of judges’ rulings declaring that the administration’s positions are contrary to the Constitution, is the leadership of the DOJ susceptible – given the Democrats have gotten the majority in the House – to impeachment for not fulfilling their oath, which requires them to support and defend the Constitution of the United States?

I don’t know that this is going to ripen to the extent that impeachment is suggested as a remedy, although arguably it could be. But I can easily see that this is going to be the subject of intensive investigations as to who ordered what and when they ordered it. And people are going to be subpoenaed and asked questions under oath that may be difficult to answer.
What is it like for these judges to be dealing with this barrage of cases that are so big and so consequential?

Typically, judges can operate under pressure; I did that many times. You’re equipped to do that as a federal judge. The real drag on the system right now is the absence of the presumption of regularity judges are being faced with. Lawyers are failing to tell the truth under direct questioning by judges. This is really an astonishing development.

Government lawyers are not litigating to the professional standards that once were the hallmark of the department. A tremendous drag on the system is caused when judges hear lawyers telling them things that simply defy belief. And they are being intentionally disingenuous as well.

And then you have to do what some judges are now doing, which is connecting the dots and issuing orders where they are expressly saying what the judge’s areas of concerns are. It’s like spoon-feeding lawyers, which judges really don’t like to do. They expect a higher degree of professionalism.
When you litigate in the federal courts, you should bring your A game – all the time. You’re playing in the big leagues.
Instead, I see minor league players being elevated into government litigators, and it’s a bad look, and it is getting worse.

articles.title: International surrogacy and the narrow legal idea of what makes a family legitimate
articles.author: Katie Tonkiss, Senior Lecturer in Sociology, Aston University
paras: A recent family court judgment in the UK highlighted ethical issues with the practice of international surrogacy. The case is thought to be the first to come before a court in the UK involving a surrogate who gave birth in China, where surrogacy is illegal. It raised numerous concerns – including about the welfare of the surrogate and child, the use of sex selection and the child’s immigration status and nationality.

Surrogacy is a growing practice in the UK, with the number of births doubling between 2015 and 2025. Most of these babies are born overseas through international surrogacy. In the UK, surrogacy is permitted only under altruistic circumstances (such as a relative or friend of the intended parents carrying the baby, with no payment beyond expenses). This can make it difficult to find a domestic surrogate.

Domestic surrogacy is prohibited across all EU member nations. But in countries such as Georgia, Ukraine and many states in the US, commercial surrogacy – where the surrogate receives payment over and above her expenses – is legal. An industry has grown around the practice.

Depending on their place of birth, babies born through international surrogacy can enter a legal grey area where their nationality is uncertain. In some cases, this can lead to the risk of statelessness because of discrepancies in how legal parenthood – and therefore often nationality – are recognised.

Where commercial surrogacy is legal, a surrogate may not be recognised as having legal parenthood of a child at all. But when a family seeks to return to their country of residence with the child, if surrogacy is not legal in that country, then the legal parenthood of the “intended parents” may also not be recognised.
Given that legal parenthood determines nationality in most countries, this can leave children born through surrogacy without a clear claim to nationality.

In the case of the baby born in China, it was not until the child was 20 months old that the parenthood of the “intended parents”, and therefore the child’s British nationality, was established in law.

Attempts to increase regulation of surrogacy internationally have stalled because of disagreement between states over the ethical issues raised by the practice. But having no nationality, as can arise in international surrogacy, also calls into question the foundations upon which access to legal identity at birth is built.

For my new book, I researched cases of international surrogacy across Europe and North America, speaking to parents as well as surrogates. I found that ideas about what counts as a “legitimate” family shape decisions about what citizenship, if any, a child should have at birth.
What is a ‘legitimate’ family?
The idea of “legitimate” and “illegitimate” families has become almost obsolete in other areas of the law. But it persists when it comes to establishing nationality.

In European countries, nationality at birth is decided by the parent or parents’ nationality. The child effectively inherits it from the parents. A number of high-profile cases before the European Court of Human Rights have sought to ensure that no child born through surrogacy could be rendered stateless, despite the prohibition of the practice across EU member states.

But I found that despite this, decisions about legal parenthood – and therefore nationality – continue to be shaped by gendered assumptions about what counts as parenthood. Specifically, the need for a gestating mother and a father who is biologically related to the child is central. I also found that, even where countries have laws to protect children born through surrogacy, LGBTQ+ parents may face obstacles in registering births, because of the absence of a gestational mother in the paperwork.

In the US, nationality typically is decided by birth on US soil. However, in cases of international surrogacy – where the child is born overseas – a child may inherit their citizenship from a parent who is a US citizen.

A series of cases before the US Supreme Court showed how stricter standards were applied to the children of LGBTQ+ couples born through international surrogacy. They were assumed to be born “out of wedlock”, despite their parents being married.

These children struggled to obtain US nationality as a result. The court ruled to prevent this discrimination, but this work has reinforced the importance of marriage to parenthood. That is, it focused on the legitimacy of the marriages, rather than the relevance of marriage to parenthood.
While ethical debates around surrogacy are unlikely to be resolved any time soon, children continue to face the risk of statelessness.

States that oppose surrogacy argue that strict rules are needed to prevent exploitation, the commodification of children and human trafficking. These concerns are very real. Yet growing numbers of children are being born through international surrogacy and face the risk of statelessness.

Addressing this requires not only renewed efforts at regulation, but also a fundamental rethink of nationality laws. So often, these tie a child’s legal identity to narrow ideas of what counts as a “legitimate” family.

articles.title: Andy Burnham at Prime Minister’s Questions: what’s he doing differently?
articles.author: Lauren Martin, Research Associate, University of Sheffield
paras: Prime Minister Andy Burnham promised from the start that he will do things differently. Whether on social care, electoral reform or ranking pub snacks with Chancellor John Healey in a video for Number 10’s social media channels, Burnham wants voters to believe he is committed to a new way of politics. In part, this means that he wants a process that is more about collaboration and problem-solving than point-scoring.

Burnham laid out this ambition in his first speech as prime minister outside Downing Street. But one major challenge to this new ethos is the Punch and Judy show that is Prime Minister’s Questions (PMQs).

My research explores the dynamics between politicians, as well as between politicians and the public. PMQs is the big moment of theatre in the parliamentary week – the one dedicated session where the prime minister is expected to answer questions from parliament. And it is the only opportunity that most MPs have to question the prime minister directly.
For his part, Burnham has also promised a “People’s Major Questions” session on social media, to answer questions from the public after PMQs.

It can be an important mechanism for parliamentary scrutiny and public accountability – 82% of people in the UK are aware of PMQs. But the event is often criticised for its noisy clashes between the prime minister and the leader of the opposition.

It has come to epitomise the adversarial nature of politics in the Commons, and researchers have found that impoliteness, verbal jabs and personal attacks are now expected in this arena. Research into broader perceptions of PMQs finds that the public has a negative opinion of it and see it as a poor example of how to behave.
Back in 2005, future prime minister David Cameron said that he was fed up of the “name-calling, backbiting, point-scoring and finger-pointing” at Westminster.

But as Conservative leader, he soon got sucked into the rowdiness and was later called the rudest prime minister at PMQs. This came after he called the then-shadow chancellor Ed Balls a “muttering idiot” (later withdrawn for unparliamentary language) and likened Ed Miliband, then leader of the opposition, to Wallace of Wallace and Gromit fame.

MPs themselves recognise that language in Westminster matters. Burnham’s attempt to reshape politics comes in the context of a general coarsening of political rhetoric that has been linked to the rise of something called “affective polarisation” (when disagreeing with opponents starts to become part of someone’s identity).

During the summer, the leader of the opposition, Kemi Badenoch, was criticised for describing then-education secretary Bridget Phillipson as a “spiteful class warrior”. She had already likened her to a “Gestapo officer” for ending tax exemption on private schools.

And Reform UK spokesman Zia Yusuf used the word “traitor” to describe former defence secretary Ben Wallace over his role in the Afghan relocation scheme in 2021. It was an example of a broader toxicity in public life, that even prompted party leader Nigel Farage to reject Yusuf’s choice of word.
Burnham avoids point-scoring … for now

So how is Burnham holding up in the PMQs arena? The timings of the summer and conference recesses mean that in his first 100 days Burnham faced only four PMQs. His fifth coincided with Healey’s first budget, and it appears to be a case of so far, so good.

Burnham is yet to be sucked into the political point-scoring that has so often plagued PMQs. He has pointed fingers at previous Conservative governments for their failings (Liz Truss’s disastrous mini-budget, for example). But the criticism is often accompanied by promises to fix the issues and an acceptance of the challenges and a need to confront them collaboratively.

This pattern has been most prevalent in his commitment to reform social care. On this, he has repeatedly appealed to working across the floor of the House, and has noted the need to do so to restore the esteem of politicians in the minds of voters.

Interestingly, Burnham has so far chosen not to attack members of other parties where his predecessors may have. At his first PMQs on September 2, as Reform UK was embroiled in various scandals about the party’s finances, Reform MP Danny Kruger asked Burnham a question about youth employment. Rather than attack Kruger over the finances, Burnham answered his question in good faith.
Burnham won praise for this decision, and he used PMQs to congratulate Badenoch on her speech at the Conservative party conference.
These are positive trends, which suggest that Burnham is taking his promises about PMQs seriously. In moments when he could have been sucked into the old noisy clashes, so far he has chosen not to.

The jeering and jibes from the benches continue (and Burnham has done “People’s Major Questions” only once). But in many ways the respect that he and Badenoch have shown one another thus far is unusual.

While it is too early to tell how long this will last – there may be many head-to-heads between now and the next general election – there are glimmers of hope for those who dislike the adversarial nature of PMQs and politics at Westminster. In an era of deep distrust in politicians, language and behaviour in parliament matter. Burnham (and Badenoch) has an opportunity to reimagine how this element of how politics at Westminster works.

articles.title: 25 years of the Police Service of Northern Ireland: the leadership and culture challenges that remain
articles.author: Joanne Murphy, Professor of Inclusive Leadership, Birmingham Business School, University of Birmingham, University of Birmingham
paras: During the 30 years of the Troubles, policing in Northern Ireland was a major area of division. The Good Friday agreement brought big changes in policing and justice, including the creation of the Police Service of Northern Ireland. This replaced the Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC), 25 years ago on November 4 2001.

At the time of the agreement in 1998, only around 8% of the RUC was Catholic – a community which made up roughly 40% of Northern Ireland’s population. While the IRA’s campaign to target and kill police officers undoubtedly deterred Catholic participation, so did the perceived unionist orientation of the organisation itself.

The agreement resulted in the Independent Commission on Policing, chaired by Conservative politician Chris Patten. This recommended a “new start” – a police service which would be representative and have the confidence of both communities.
Following radical structural and symbolic change, the police service has become arguably the most successful institutional achievement of the wider peace process.

Changes included a new name, badge, and an extraordinarily expensive voluntary severance scheme (costing roughly £500 million). A time-limited recruitment strategy involved the appointment of new officers on a controversial 50% Catholic and 50% “other” basis.
Undoubtedly, the organisation has transformed from its RUC inheritance. At the time of writing, about 31% of police officers are Catholic.

Evidence shows 91.5% of people in Northern Ireland feel safe in their community. And nearly three-quarters view the PSNI as effective in keeping areas safe. Around 92% of respondents felt confident contacting the PSNI if needed, and roughly 65% feel the police service represents their community. But importantly, unionists had more confidence in policing (73.8%) and nationalists less so (58.2%). The force also enjoys the backing of all political parties in Northern Ireland.

But policing is still buffeted by politics, both present and past and lower confidence among nationalists is indicative of concerns that remain 25 years after the Patten commission. A series of internal and external controversies have exacerbated this.

The resignation of PSNI chief constable Simon Byrne in 2023 was the result of a contentious and difficult series of events around the policing of a Troubles commemoration during a COVID lockdown. The organisation came as close as it ever has to being in complete crisis. The legacy of the past, concerns in the present and the still-divided Northern Irish community have all played a part.
In addition, Catholic applications are dropping precipitately and some political parties are calling for a “Patten II” amid concerns that the organisation has lost its way.

While the PSNI has been hoping for an application rate of around 50% from Catholics, only 26.7% of applications in a recent recruitment drive were from Catholics. As one young Catholic woman commented wryly during my research: “Sure, that’s not even a pass mark.”

My research with Jess Bonnan-White suggests several ongoing issues. They are organisational, rather than political. The most significant is its relationship – organisationally, historically and psychologically – with its RUC past.
Transformation and challenges

The incorporation of the RUC into the PSNI was a substantive issue when the service was created in 2001. Those who held an affinity to the RUC had argued for the preservation of its legacy. One outcome was that the RUC name was incorporated into the title deeds of the PSNI.

Transformation was obvious in the outward-facing sense – changes to the force’s name, symbols and uniform. But the RUC culture was preserved in the material reality of the police estate, commemorative medals, artefacts in the Newforge sports complex (which is still home to the RUC Athletic Association), and the norms and attitudes within the service.

It is perhaps the culture in which the past is most evident. As former PSNI chief constable George Hamilton said in 2019: “Around 80% of the current police service were never in the RUC, but when you … see the photographs on the walls, when you listen to the stories in the police canteen, you’d think it was the opposite.”
This pairing of outward change and internal continuity has created an inherent tension and a cultural confusion. At times, this has actively hampered the service’s transformation.

Additionally, high-profile inquiries, including into atrocities such as the 1992 Sean Graham bookmaker shop murders, and accusations of RUC collusion, have dogged the PSNI. As the RUC was incorporated into the establishment of the PSNI, it has been difficult to fully separate the old from the new.

Since it was established, the PSNI has lost two officers to dissident republican violence. It is fortunate not to have lost more. Our research suggests that the murders of Catholic officers Stephen Carroll and Ronan Kerr, and incidents that were foiled have fundamentally altered the trajectory of how “policing with the community” can be implemented.

In returning to a security mindset, the PSNI has been unable to integrate itself authentically into both communities, as envisaged by the Patten reforms. Such attacks have also acted as a major disincentive to Catholic recruits, exacerbating the challenge within the nationalist community.

A culture of fear internally and wariness externally have been compounded by organisational mistakes, such as the enormous 2023 data leak, which saw the names and roles of all staff briefly disclosed online.

For Catholics, policing can still mean alienation from their communities and families. There are also significant concerns internally about psychological safety – and worries that Catholic officers do not feel protected by the organisation.

Other fears – concerns around promotion and advancement, evidence of greater referrals of Catholic officers to professional standards, perceived inadequate transmission of intelligence to allow officers to keep themselves safe, as well as other forms of sectarianism – have come up in my discussions with officers.

Undoubtedly, the organisation faces significant structural problems. Brutal funding cuts, low officer numbers and a policing environment that is still volatile have all reduced the appetite for risk. While some of these challenges are common to policing in both Great Britain and the Irish Republic, the PSNI’s own research suggests that it has been hit much harder by financial cuts than comparative forces.

Despite these challenges, the PSNI has proved extraordinarily resilient. Ironically, the elements that underpinned this resilience – structures, history and organisational memory – have also been why it has struggled to build and maintain the confidence of the Catholic community.
The PSNI may have transformed from its RUC past, but it is still policing a divided society.

articles.title: Disaster aid has become a political lottery – libraries, schools and places of worship are stepping into the breach
articles.author: Daniel P. Aldrich, Professor of Political Science, Public Policy and Urban Affairs, Northeastern University
paras: Four tornadoes tore across southwest Michigan in early March 2026, killing four people. They were the state’s deadliest natural hazards in decades.
Gov. Gretchen Whitmer asked the Federal Emergency Management Agency for assistance to cover uninsured and underinsured losses. FEMA said no. She appealed. FEMA said no again.

I study how communities prepare for and recover from disasters. As Dean’s Professor of Resilience at Northeastern University, I have written six books on the topic, including the forthcoming “Beyond Common Ground.”
The fact that Michigan was repeatedly denied aid reflects a broader shift, one that is putting more weight on the ties between neighbors and the places where they meet.
Federal help is less predictable
The Trump administration denied 26% of major disaster declarations in 2025, more than double the rate of the year before and well above the 15% denial average of the past two decades.

Denials have not fallen evenly. One study looked at some 2,500 disaster declarations since FEMA’s creation in 1979 in states where the governor and U.S. senators were all Republican or all Democrat. In his second term, Trump approved nearly 90% of requests from all-Republican states while approving only 23% of those from all-Democratic states.
Colorado, an all-Democratic state, had both of its 2025 appeals for disaster rejected. They were Colorado’s first denials since the 1980s.

Florida, an all-Republican state, fared differently. In June, Trump announced US$416 million for the state’s disasters without specifying which one, adding that much of it would go to the Panhandle, one of his “favorite places.” There, a January 2025 snowstorm was linked to 13 deaths and caused approximately $200 million in damages.

Nationally, an analysis of FEMA data by Andrew Rumbach, a senior fellow at the Urban Institute, found that about 84% of requests from states Trump won in 2024 were approved during his second term, compared with about 42% from states he lost.

While the White House has denied that politics plays a role in who receives aid after shocks, local communities are now shouldering more of the cost of preparing for, responding to and recovering from disasters than they did before 2025.

FEMA owes local governments almost $10 billion in reimbursements for recovery work that cities and towns have already paid for. When a declaration is denied, towns can be left covering costs as high as 15% of their annual budget. Philanthropies and aid groups such as Team Rubicon are expanding their roles to fill the gaps.
Nonprofits and community organizations cannot replace federal funding, but they can build cooperation, trust and collective action, which can better prepare neighborhoods and accelerate recovery.
In Union City, Michigan, help arrived within hours of the EF3 tornado that killed three people in March 2026. It came not from Washington but from neighbors.
School administrators turned the local high school into a shelter the night of the storm, volunteers arrived with food and supplies, and the local United Way opened a relief fund.
That is typical: Local residents are almost always the first responders after disasters strike. What was different is that federal help never followed.

Donations poured into the local high school, and the superintendent said staff worked out how to get supplies to the people who needed them. A local church, damaged in the storm, started a disaster fund to help residents pay their insurance deductibles.
Research on U.S. disasters shows how places such as schools, faith-based organizations and libraries can keep communities knit together.

After Hurricane Katrina in August 2005, floodwaters as high as 12 feet (3.6 meters) covered the low-income neighborhood around the Mary Queen of Vietnam Church in east New Orleans. Yet by summer 2007, about 90% of its residents had returned to their homes. For the city as a whole, the figure hit only 45%. The difference was likely the leadership of the Rev. Vien Nguyen, who coordinated supplies, organized volunteers and kept scattered residents in touch even as they evacuated to other states.

My lab’s research during the COVID-19 pandemic found a similar pattern. We compared U.S. counties that were alike in many ways but differed in their social ties. After accounting for politics, governance, healthcare quality and demographics, our study found that two kinds of ties reduced the pandemic’s toll: bonding ties and linking ties.
Bonding ties connect neighbors and family.
Linking ties connect residents to officials. Those ties are often built through spaces designed for connection, such as libraries and faith-based organizations like Nguyen’s church in New Orleans.
Libraries continue to safeguard our most vulnerable. In 2025, 44.7% of U.S. public libraries served as cooling or warming centers during extreme temperatures, up 8.2% from 2022.

Many could do more. In a national survey, 84% of library directors agreed that libraries have a critical role in disaster response. Yet only 36% knew that federal law allows libraries to seek FEMA relocation funding to move to safer ground, and just 51% had an emergency preparedness plan.
A low-cost layer of protection

In my new book, I show that more than 90% of federal disaster funds went to roads, utilities and other standard infrastructure in the early 21st century, and less than 10% to libraries, parks, schools, places of worship and community centers, where neighbors check on one another and organize recovery.
Federal aid may go to rebuild some of these spaces, but it rarely pays to keep them open and running when communities need them most.

In another study, I found that Japanese communities with higher density of social infrastructure had half the number of deaths from a catastrophic tsunami in March 2011 compared to similar communities with fewer gathering spaces.

In my assessment, as federal aid becomes less predictable, these kinds of places people frequent often will have to carry us into the future. The communities that recover best from the next disaster may be the ones that kept their libraries open, their civic halls full of volunteers and their parks full of residents.

articles.title: The history of royal tours shows why they’re important for the monarchy – despite the risk of uncomfortable questions
articles.author: Alice Hunt, Professor of Early Modern Literature and History, University of Southampton
paras: The royal tour of the Caribbean is the king’s first visit to this region of the Commonwealth as monarch. It comes at a time of protests and growing demands for slavery reparations, as well as an apology for the royal family’s historic role in the trade.

Against this backdrop, historian Anthony Seldon described this tour as potentially “the biggest risk” of the king’s reign. Charles is in the region not just as a head of state and of the Commonwealth, but as the head of a family that personally benefited from slavery.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also travelled to the Caribbean for the Commonwealth heads of government summit. Burnham has said he is open to the idea of an apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade, but has made clear that he does not believe reparations are the right answer.

The last time Charles visited the Caribbean was in November 2021, to oversee the transition of Barbados to a republic. The Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, on the schedule this time, are among the eight Caribbean nations which retain the British monarch as head of state. Guyana, also part of the tour, became a republic in 1970.

The king knew he could not escape uncomfortable exchanges on this tour. There is increasing local pressure from the Caribbean Reparations Commission on Charles to offer a formal apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade. On the king’s first night in the Bahamas, at a youth rally in the capital Nassau, he referred to “the great suffering and injustices of the past”. There were some protesters, but they remained outside.

Royal tours have always been risky. After the last royal visit to the Caribbean, to mark the platinum jubilee in 2022, the traditional format looked to be in need of a rethink. “Tone deaf” images of William and Kate in Jamaica, dressed in imperial white in an open-top Jamaica Defence Force Land Rover, and greeting children through a wire fence went viral.

It was a jarring reminder of the colonial past, overshadowing the entire tour, which also saw protests in Belize and the Bahamas. Afterwards, William said that foreign tours offered “an opportunity to reflect”.
The historic role of the tour

The risks of this autumn’s tour will have been weighed carefully by the Royal Visits Committee (part of the Cabinet Office). The history of the royal tour can explain why the risks were considered to be worth taking.

As part of “The Visible Crown” research project, I have examined the royal family’s connections to the Caribbean, looking in particular at visits since Elizabeth II took the throne in 1952. What I’ve found is that the survival of the monarchy in the Caribbean can in part be explained by the history of its carefully managed visibility.
The royal visit as we know it was invented to legitimise the Commonwealth and sustain the British monarchy during the period of imperial decline and constitutional change.

For some of the islands, Elizabeth’s tour to the Caribbean in 1966 was the first time a monarch had ever visited. At that time, officials threshed out their “philosophy of the royal visit”. They knew that the tours needed to present an image of Elizabeth that would make sense of her role in countries that had either become newly independent, or were about to become independent, as well as in those that might choose to become republics.

That image would be as the mother figure for the new “family of nations” – the Commonwealth. The royal tour has remained largely unchanged since: visits should be short, but frequent – a change from the longer imperial tours. They should have the feel of a family party and the monarch must be easily visible.

Informality and accessibility were priorities: garden parties, walkabouts in the sun and street celebrations as well as the more sombre guards of honour and speeches in the host nation’s parliament would become staples.

The formulaic itineraries endorsed the values of continuity, protection and compassion. Children were always involved – visits to children’s homes, schools and hospitals afford opportunities to show a caring, healing monarch invested in their future.
Official footage of the 1966 Caribbean tour pauses on a child in St Lucia holding a placard: “We love you, come back soon”.

The choreographers of royal tours are aware of the strange capacity for these rituals to rouse emotion and cultivate loyalty. After Elizabeth’s visit to Jamaica in 1983, the country’s high commissioner reported back to the British government that “the warmth of popular feeling” generated by her visit demonstrated “afresh the widespread attachment to the crown”. Charles now has to remake the royal tour in his own image. But in fact, his age is on his side, lending him vulnerability.

As my work on the history of royal ceremonies has shown, the British monarchy has always deployed and adapted symbols, rituals and pageantry to legitimise itself and sustain significance in a changing world. The modern Commonwealth tour and its insistence on visibility is informed by the early modern tradition of the royal progress. Elizabeth I, like Elizabeth II, knew that she had to be “seen to be believed”, and frequently moved through London and around the country greeting subjects. Then, as now, there were protests as well as cheers.

In the context of the Caribbean however, a tour’s display of royal power reinforces a complex and longstanding alignment between supposedly legitimate authority and whiteness. But constitutional reform was also part of the agenda of this current trip. Several Caribbean leaders have recently stated their intention for their nations to become republics: Jamaica, Bahamas, and Antigua and Barbuda.

But as a recent survey by researchers at the University of West Indies has revealed, support for republicanism varies significantly between nations. It is not strong enough, according to many of the constitutions, to bring about reform.

The king’s (unelected) role as head of the Commonwealth matters to him, as it did to his mother. This position preserves the global status of the British monarchy. This tour was an opportunity, then, to bind the Caribbean Commonwealth, and to legitimise Charles as its father figure. He may not need to say sorry for Britain’s role in slavery for this trip to be considered a success.
This article was updated on November 3 to amend some details about the constitutional arrangements of the countries visited on this tour.
Alice Hunt receives funding from The Arts and Humanities Research Council.

articles.title: From 18th-century false ballots to the second JFK and double Dan Sullivans, a brief history of spoiler candidates and the unsuccessful legal challenges to them
articles.author: Drew Kurlowski, Associate Professor of Political Science, Coastal Carolina University
paras: Less than a week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that people with links to Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola’s U.S. Senate campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee had recruited a candidate to the race whose name is nearly identical to that of the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, whom Peltola was challenging. The plan aimed to siphon votes from the incumbent senator and help Peltola win, according to the reporting.

The story has driven calls for prosecutions, lawsuits and state action. But as a political scientist who studies election law, I can say that the spoiler candidate is one of the oldest tricks in the American campaign toolbox, and the law has rarely touched it.
For most of the 1800s, American elections were conducted with ballots designed and printed by the parties. There were no official ballots printed by the state.

In those days, the addition of a rival name to a party ballot by an insidious printer could swing countless votes to the opposing party. The tactic was well known, and voters were often warned to look out for the “Spurious Ticket.”
By the 1890s, the government-printed ballot had gained widespread adoption and ended the practice of counterfeit tickets. But that would not be enough to deter those who wanted to deceive voters.
As observers in Alaska have noted, recruiting candidates with similar or identical names is not a new move.

In John F. Kennedy’s first congressional primary, his opponent was a city councilor named Joseph Russo. An aide to Kennedy reportedly paid a janitor with the same name to enter the race. The real Russo complained, but in the end, Kennedy took more votes in the 1946 race than the Russos combined.

Eight years later, the name Kennedy worked the other way, when a Gillette stockroom supervisor named John Francis Kennedy, no relation, was elected as a Democrat to the position of treasurer and receiver-general of Massachusetts, owing in large part to the familiarity of his name. Names can move votes, so namesakes can be worth recruiting.
Some spoiler candidates are not necessarily meant to win votes. Sometimes they are there to amplify a message.

In 1978, Republican Carroll Campbell was running for an open House seat in upstate South Carolina. His opponent was Max Heller, the mayor of Greenville and a Jewish refugee from Nazi-occupied Austria.

Days before the election, Don Sprouse, an independent running for office for the first time, held a press conference and declared that Heller was unfit for office as he had “not made clear to the voters he is not a Christian” and was “not as qualified to represent the Christian people.”

Although Campbell condemned the remarks and Sprouse received only 1,693 votes, Heller lost the race. The allegations, still unproven, of Sprouse being a “stalking-horse” for Campbell only surfaced years later, but they continued to dog Campbell when he ran for governor in 1986.
Sprouse wasn’t going to spoil the election with the votes he could win, but he could be a spoiler with his message, an antisemitic appeal that Campbell would not make directly.
Candidates who don’t even know they’re running
A different type of ballot shenanigan skips the recruitment and simply puts candidates on the ballot.

This was the case in 2010 when two Oakland County, Michigan, Democratic officials put candidates on the ballot under the Tea Party label in three races. The candidates didn’t even know they were running.
In this case, the law did come back to bite. The county party chair and operations director were charged with perjury and forgery, but the crime was forging signatures, not their strategy.

Some state election codes specifically discuss false declarations or forged election paperwork, but many don’t contemplate this type of scheme. Forgery and perjury, however, are illegal across the country, and it’s almost impossible to put an unwitting person on the ballot without one or the other.

In Alaska, this tactic can be used cheaply. There is no petition requirement to get on the ballot, just a $100 fee. Moreover, the parties can’t vet candidates in the primary. The state’s unique top-four primary system lets candidates choose their own party label.
The saga of Daniel J. Sullivan, the schoolteacher known as “Petersburg Sullivan” because of where he lives, and Sen. Dan S. Sullivan goes back longer than recent revelations.

Petersburg Sullivan filed to run as a Republican in the Senate race just three days before the deadline; state officials tried to bar him from the ballot. In June a judge said there was nothing in Alaska law to prevent him from appearing on the ballot, and the state Supreme Court subsequently agreed.

Since he couldn’t be removed, the state Division of Elections took unusual steps on their ballot design to help distinguish the two candidates. They listed Sen. Dan S. Sullivan as a Republican, marking him as the incumbent, and left Daniel J. Sullivan without a party designation. This had not been done for previous incumbents in at least a decade.

Assuming there is no forgery of documents with an unwitting and unwilling spoiler candidate, there is little the law can do. History shows us that the real legal exposure in these cases usually lies where it most often does in politics: money.

In a 2020 Miami, Florida, race, a former state senator turned political operative was convicted of three felonies related to efforts to recruit and pay a decoy candidate with the same surname as the Democratic incumbent. In another Florida case, a local Republican Party chair was convicted in connection with a scheme to plant a progressive alternative to siphon votes from the Democratic candidate. In both cases the prosecutions focused on campaign finance crimes, not simply on putting the spoilers on the ballot.

The state of Washington is an outlier, where it is a felony to run under a rival’s surname if the intent is to confuse voters. In 2024, two Bob Fergusons were recruited by conservative activist Glen Morgan to run for governor against state Attorney General Bob Ferguson. Both opted to drop out of their race under threat of prosecution.

There is nothing comparable to these laws in Alaska, however, and whether laws like this could prevent this type of thing in a federal election is still untested. Under the Supreme Court’s decision in U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton in 1995, states cannot add their own qualifications for Congress.

The advice from 1860 – “Watch your tickets on election day. There’s a scheme on foot …” – when newspapers urged voters to read their tickets before casting their vote, is still relevant long after the demise of the party ticket. It is unlikely that the law can solve this problem, because to do so would be to wade into the First Amendment waters of why people run for office. Regulating thought and intention is a dangerous proposition under the Constitution.
The old answer is the best one. Self-government depends less on clever rules and more on citizens paying attention. Read your ballots!

articles.title: Are American voters actually gloomy about the economy, or is something else going on?
articles.author: Erin Kay Lockwood, Assistant Professor of Political Science, University of California, Irvine
paras: Polling is looking grim for Republicans ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, 2026, due in large part to deep pessimism among the public about the economy.

At first glance, this might seem surprising. With the exception of inflation, many economic measures remain strong, including gross domestic product growth. But consumer sentiment continues to languish.
This has prompted a debate over whether mere “vibes” are in play, or whether these long-used metrics are no longer capturing something fundamental to Americans’ economic well-being.

This debate matters politically because voters are placing an overwhelming priority on the economy as an issue in the midterms. A Pew Research survey in early October 2026 found that 84% of registered voters said the economy was very important to their vote, and the concern is bipartisan. Among the issues in that Pew survey, for example, “the economy” was the least polarizing, with 82% of Republicans and 88% of Democrats ranking it as very important.

Meanwhile, the overall drop in voters’ economic outlook has largely been driven by growing pessimism among Republicans. While Democrats remain much gloomier about the economy than Republicans, the gap is narrowing.

These trends help explain why Democrats are expected to make significant gains in Congress: This election will likely be seen as an indictment of how well the economy is working for ordinary Americans under President Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress, despite strong macroeconomic measures.

As a scholar of financial markets and global inequality, I believe the relationship between how people see their own finances and their view of the broader economy is also changing on a more fundamental level. And this shift will affect how they judge the next class of lawmakers in power.

When scholars try to understand how people judge the economy – and how they separate their own personal circumstances from the broader economy – one of their key reference points is the University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index. It asks respondents about their personal finances, their short-term and long-term economic outlook, and whether they think it’s a good time to make major purchases.

This gauge has historically tracked key economic measures of consumer spending and inflation: The state of the broader economy usually shapes the way people think about their own financial well-being.
But in recent years, these have diverged. By many measures, the economy is doing well, but people feel they’re falling behind. And this has only become more pronounced ahead of the midterms.
Despite strong consumer spending, robust business investment and low unemployment, consumer sentiment keeps slipping and is now 10% below where it was a year ago, according to the Michigan index.

Some commentators point to ongoing inflation as the reason for gloom. It has remained stubbornly above the Federal Reserve’s annual 2% target rate due to drivers like tariffs, energy price hikes stemming from Middle East turmoil, and massive amounts of investment in the artificial intelligence build-out.

But what’s really happening is that consumer sentiment data and inflation data have become untethered. Inflation has actually dropped sharply from its 21st-century peak of 9.1% in June 2022 after the pandemic to 3.7% in September 2026, but consumer sentiment is lower now than it was even then.

What about wages? Here, too, the data also doesn’t fully explain this disconnect. While inflation makes consumer goods pricier, it also lifts pay. Inflation-adjusted wages actually increased between 2022 and the first half of 2026, all while consumer sentiment remained weak. What has changed in recent months is that inflation-adjusted wages are now falling – which could help explain the darkening outlook among voters.
One possibility is that deeply entrenched inequality explains this divergence.

Compared with other eras of moderate-to-high inflation, the U.S. economy today is much more unequal. Income inequality has increased over the past 20 years, narrowing only during the 2008 and 2020 crises before quickly widening to prior levels.

This trend is important for understanding which consumers are shelling out cash. The Fed has consistently cited strong consumer spending in its economic assessments, but the richest 10% of Americans account for half of that spending today. Meanwhile, spending by the bottom 80% of earners has fallen behind inflation.

In other words, the strong total consumer spending figures reported as official data are being driven by very wealthy Americans and fail to reflect the experience of typical consumers who are the bulk of the electorate.

This trend of increasing inequality has been particularly acute in terms of wealth: The top 0.1% of American households together own five times as much wealth as the bottom 50%. Much of this reflects the uneven gains of the stock market boom and how wealth is taxed.
In short, Americans’ economic malaise might be driven by concerns over income and wealth that conventional measures don’t fully capture.
When it comes to consumer surveys like the University of Michigan index, economists generally assume that the answers reflect the personal experience of respondents.

But I agree with other scholars who argue that sometimes these answers may be based less on people’s own circumstances and more on how they view the economy as a whole. This assessment could reflect, for example, concerns like equity, equality of opportunity and economic justice.
When responses are driven by a concern for collective well-being rather than just personal material self-interest, social scientists refer to such perceptions as “sociotropic.”

This last point isn’t just theoretical. Research suggests voters tend to weight their perceptions of the economy more heavily than their personal financial circumstances when deciding whether to vote for the incumbent party.

Trade is one good example. Americans’ preferences for trade policy are driven less by how a particular measure, like tariffs, would impact them personally and more by how they think it would affect the country as a whole.

If consumer sentiment follows a similar path, that could explain the divergence between generally strong economic trends and weak consumer sentiment. People are thinking not just about their own conditions but those of the U.S. as a whole, and it’s possible that their understanding of “the economy” includes its relationship to inequality.

Understanding the disconnect between the economic data traditionally used to assess the economy’s health and Americans’ perceptions of that economy is important not just to the scholars trying to make sense of it – it could also help set an agenda for the incoming Congress. If economic insecurity punishes the governing party at the polls, the next Congress will be expected to do something about it once sworn in.

Voters generally back the incumbent party when the economy is doing well and the out-party when it’s not. But how they judge the health of the economy is not straightforward, and the past six years suggest that improving headline measures of economic health – without regard to Americans’ lived experience and their concerns about what kind of economy is being built – may not be enough to assuage voters’ concerns.
